paragraphs.text: Animals interact with other members of their own species in a wide variety of ways. Some animals, such as hamsters, are largely solitary in their behaviour, only coming together when they mate. Other animals form groups of varying size and structure. For example, shoals of fish are essentially loose gatherings of individuals, while primates (apes and monkeys) form groups which are much more complex. A variety of roles associated with social dominance or subordination can be recognised, and there is often division of labour. Living in social groups has many advantages. Important among these is that some degree of cooperation is possible- in finding and collecting food, in looking out for danger, and in defending against predators.

One of the most basic types of social group is the nuclear family, where both of the parents remain with the young for a given period of time. Many songbirds are an example of this. Some other birds- mallard ducks for instance-and many mammals, such as bears, form one-parent families, where parental care is undertaken by females, while in the case of certain amphibians, it is the male that guards the young.

Extended families are formed when the offspring remain and help rear succeeding generations. Ants, termites, and some bees and wasps are unusual examples of extended families, because they live in such large groups and exhibit a very strict division of labour. In the case of bees, all females except the queen remain sterile because of a hormone produced by the queen, while males are required only to fertilize new queens. In a group of termites, specific tasks are performed by different castes-the queen, who lays the eggs, and sterile, wingless workers and soldiers. Every so often, males and females with wings are produced, which are capable of reproduction. These leave the nest to start new colonies. The naked mole rat-a species of rodent that lives in large groups in underground burrows-exhibits a similar type of social organization. Only one pair breeds. Small, non-breeding animals of either sex dig the tunnels, while larger ones stay near the breeding female, feeding her and taking care of the young.

Harems are composed of a single breeding male and a group of females, each with her own young. Permanent harems are formed by animals such as zebra and patas monkeys. Other animals, such as red deer, form temporary harems that only stay together for the duration of the breeding season. For the rest of the year, the females and their young generally form female groups. The males either live in bachelor herds-as is the case with red deer-or they may live alone. Multi-male groups are formed by several animals, including common baboons, hyenas and lions. A number of males and females in these groups breed, although there may be a hierarchy in both sexes to determine which animals breed most often, and when they do so. At adolescence, male baboons frequently leave their home groups and join another group. A male lion may abandon its own group to take over another group of females by force.

Monogamous pairing, where one male mates with a single female, is particularly common in birds, where males are needed to rear the young. In spite of the vast size of their nesting colonies, penguins usually return to their mate of the previous year, each parent taking it in turns to incubate the eggs. After their initial rearing, the chicks join groups of their contemporaries in communal nurseries, usually preside over by a few adults.

The social organization of a species is not rigidly fixed. As with red deer, it often changes with the season. Many garden birds live in pairs only during the summer; in winter, species such as chaffinches and starlings live in large flocks, while robins, for instance, live alone.

Furthermore, whatever form of social organization is most common for a particular species, it is sometimes necessary for one or more animals to keep a particular area for their sole use. In these cases, they keep out other members of the same species. An area in which vital resources such as food or shelter are defended in this way is known as a territory. Territories may be held by any number of animals: hamsters and mice, for instance, hold their territories singly; gulls in pairs; hyenas, lions and prairie dogs in larger groups. Many animals patrol the boundaries of their territories regularly and attack any intruder, using various signals to indicate their possession of a territory. A territory is only worth defending if the benefits-in terms of food obtained or young successfully reared-outweigh the cost. The golden-winged sunbird, for instance, defends a territory containing its food source, nectar from Leonotis flowers. The energy it obtains from the flowers just exceeds that used in the process of feeding and in defending the territory, so the bird makes a small net gain.
